**1. 印度尼西亚的首都：雅加达（Jakarta）**
雅加达是印度尼西亚最大的城市和经济中心，位于爪哇岛西北部。

**2. 巴基斯坦的首都：伊斯兰堡（Islamabad）**
伊斯兰堡是巴基斯坦的政治首都，位于该国北部，是一个规划建设的现代城市。

**3. 巴西的首都：巴西利亚（Brasília）**
巴西利亚是巴西的行政首都，这座位于巴西中部的城市是上世纪中期为发展内陆地区而专门规划和建设的首都。

**4. 尼日利亚的首都：阿布贾（Abuja）**
阿布贾是尼日利亚的政治首都，位于该国中心地带，1991年从拉各斯迁都至此。

**5. 美国的首都：华盛顿（Washington, D.C.）**
华盛顿哥伦比亚特区是美国的首都，位于东海岸，是为美国联邦政府专门设立的特殊行政区。

这五个首都中，巴西利亚、阿布贾和华盛顿都是专门规划建设的首都城市，而非自然发展形成的传统城市。

On 17 January 2022, the name was revealed to be Nusantara.[5]


The plan is part of a strategy to reduce developmental inequality between Java and other islands in the Indonesian archipelago and to reduce Jakarta's burden as Indonesia's primary hub.[6][7][8] In August 2019, the government announced that while the capital will be moved, $40 billion will be spent on saving Jakarta from sinking in the next decade.[9]

<title>List of countries and dependencies by population</title>
<fragment>
This article reflects continually changing information from hundreds of sources. You can help by updating items to more recent figures from official sources.

![](image)Cartogram of the world's population in 2018; each square represents 500,000 people.
This is a **list of countries and dependencies by population**. It includes sovereign states, inhabited dependent territories and, in some cases, constituent countries of sovereign states, with inclusion within the list being primarily based on the ISO standard ISO 3166-1. For instance, the United Kingdom is considered a single entity, while the constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands are considered separately. In addition, this list includes certain states with limited recognition not found in ISO 3166-1. **Tokyo** (/ˈtoʊkioʊ/;[7] Template:Lang-ja, *Tōkyō*, Template:IPA-ja), officially the **Tokyo Metropolis** (Template:Lang-ja, *Tōkyō-to*), is the capital of Japan and the most populous city in the world with a population of over 14 million residents as of 2023.[8]


The Tokyo metropolitan area, which includes Tokyo and three neighboring Japanese prefectures, Tochigi, Gunma, and Ibaraki, is 13,452 square kilometers or 5,194 square miles and the world's most-populous metropolitan area with 40.8 million residents as of 2023[update].[9]


Located at the head of Tokyo Bay, Tokyo is part of the Kantō region on the central coast of Honshu, Japan's largest island. Tokyo serves as Japan's economic center and the seat of both the Japanese government and the Emperor of Japan.

**Tokyo** (/ˈtoʊkioʊ/;[7] Template:Lang-ja, *Tōkyō*, Template:IPA-ja), officially the **Tokyo Metropolis** (Template:Lang-ja, *Tōkyō-to*), is the capital of Japan and the most populous city in the world with a population of over 14 million residents as of 2023.[8]


The Tokyo metropolitan area, which includes Tokyo and three neighboring Japanese prefectures, Tochigi, Gunma, and Ibaraki, is 13,452 square kilometers or 5,194 square miles and the world's most-populous metropolitan area with 40.8 million residents as of 2023[update].[9]


Located at the head of Tokyo Bay, Tokyo is part of the Kantō region on the central coast of Honshu, Japan's largest island. Tokyo serves as Japan's economic center and the seat of both the Japanese government and the Emperor of Japan.

The broader Seoul metropolitan area, encompassing Gyeonggi province and Incheon metropolitan city, emerged as the world's fourth largest metropolitan economy in 2014, trailing only Tokyo, New York City, and Los Angeles, hosting more than half of South Korea's population. Although Seoul's population peaked at slightly over 10 million, it has gradually decreased since 2014, standing at approximately 9.97 million residents as of 2020. **Dhaka** (/ˈdɑːkə/ *DAH-kə* or /ˈdækə/ *DAK-ə*; Template:Lang-bn, Template:IPA-bn), formerly known as **Dacca**,[15] is the capital and largest city of Bangladesh. It is the ninth-largest and seventh-most densely populated city in the world. Dhaka is a megacity, and has a population of 10.2 million residents as of 2022, and a population of over 22.4 million residents in Dhaka Metropolitan Area.[16][17][18] It is widely considered to be the most densely populated built-up urban area in the world.[19][20] Dhaka is the most important cultural, economic, and scientific hub of Eastern South Asia, as well as a major Muslim-majority city. Dhaka ranks third in South Asia and 39th in the world in terms of GDP. Lying on the Ganges Delta, it is bounded by the Buriganga, Turag, Dhaleshwari and Shitalakshya rivers. Dhaka is also the largest Bengali-speaking city in the world.

**Islamabad** (/ɪzˈlɑːməbæd/;[7] Template:Lang-ur, listenⓘ; transl. 'City of Islam') is the capital city of Pakistan.[8] It is the country's ninth-most populous city with a population of over 1.2 million people[9] and is federally administered by the Pakistani government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s, it replaced Karachi as Pakistan's official national capital. The city is notable for its high standards of living,[10] safety,[11] cleanliness, abundant greenery and architecture.[12]

**Ottawa** (/ˈɒtəwə/ ⓘ, /ˈɒtəwɑː/; Canadian French: Template:IPA-fr) is the capital city of Canada. It is located in the southern portion of the province of Ontario, at the confluence of the Ottawa River and the Rideau River. Ottawa borders Gatineau, Quebec, and forms the core of the Ottawa–Gatineau census metropolitan area (CMA) and the National Capital Region (NCR).[15] As of 2021,[update] Ottawa had a city population of 1,017,449 and a metropolitan population of 1,488,307, making it the fourth-largest city and fourth-largest metropolitan area in Canada.


Ottawa is the political centre of Canada and headquarters to the federal government. The city houses numerous foreign embassies, key buildings, organizations, and institutions of Canada's government; these include the Parliament of Canada, the Supreme Court, the residence of Canada's viceroy, and Office of the Prime Minister.[16]

**Ottawa** (/ˈɒtəwə/ ⓘ, /ˈɒtəwɑː/; Canadian French: Template:IPA-fr) is the capital city of Canada. It is located in the southern portion of the province of Ontario, at the confluence of the Ottawa River and the Rideau River. Ottawa borders Gatineau, Quebec, and forms the core of the Ottawa–Gatineau census metropolitan area (CMA) and the National Capital Region (NCR).[15] As of 2021,[update] Ottawa had a city population of 1,017,449 and a metropolitan population of 1,488,307, making it the fourth-largest city and fourth-largest metropolitan area in Canada.


Ottawa is the political centre of Canada and headquarters to the federal government. The city houses numerous foreign embassies, key buildings, organizations, and institutions of Canada's government; these include the Parliament of Canada, the Supreme Court, the residence of Canada's viceroy, and Office of the Prime Minister.[16]

## Myanmar (Burma)
**Naypyidaw** - This is the most recent major capital relocation. Myanmar moved its capital from Yangon (formerly Rangoon) to Naypyidaw in 2005-2006. The new capital was officially established in 2006 and is described as a planned city that is notably less populated than traditional capitals.

## Australia
**Canberra** - Australia chose Canberra as its capital in 1908 following the federation of the colonies, with construction beginning in 1913. This move was designed to settle the rivalry between Sydney and Melbourne by creating a purpose-built capital city.

## India  
**New Delhi** - While Delhi has long been an important city, New Delhi was specifically built to serve as the capital, with construction beginning in 1911 after the British moved the capital from Calcutta (now Kolkata). It was officially inaugurated as the capital in 1931.

## Canada
**Ottawa** - Ottawa was chosen as Canada's capital in 1857, selected by Queen Victoria to resolve conflicts between competing cities like Toronto, Montreal, and Quebec.

## United States
**Washington, D.C.** - The US capital moved from temporary locations like Philadelphia and New York to its permanent location in Washington, D.C. in 1800.

Other planned capital cities include **Brasília** (Brazil, moved from Rio de Janeiro in 1960) and **Abuja** (Nigeria, moved from Lagos in 1991), though I didn't search for these specifically.

The most dramatic recent example is Naypyidaw, Myanmar, which was built from scratch to become the capital in 2006, though it remains relatively underpopulated compared to traditional capitals.

**Islamabad** (/ɪzˈlɑːməbæd/;[7] Template:Lang-ur, listenⓘ; transl. 'City of Islam') is the capital city of Pakistan.[8] It is the country's ninth-most populous city with a population of over 1.2 million people[9] and is federally administered by the Pakistani government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s, it replaced Karachi as Pakistan's official national capital. The city is notable for its high standards of living,[10] safety,[11] cleanliness, abundant greenery and architecture.[12]

**Djibloho**, officially the **Administrative City of Djibloho**[1] (Template:Lang-es),[2] is the newest province of Equatorial Guinea, formally established by law in 2017.[3] The administrative city was initially carved out of Añisok, a district in Wele-Nzas,[4] on 1 August 2015,[5] and was created to eventually replace Malabo as Equatorial Guinea's national capital.[6]



## Administration

[edit]

![A clickable map of Equatorial Guinea exhibiting its two regions and eight provinces. The island nation of São Tomé and Príncipe is not part of Equatorial Guinea.](image)A clickable map of Equatorial Guinea exhibiting its two regions and eight provinces. The island nation of São Tomé and Príncipe is not part of Equatorial Guinea.
Djibloho comprises two urban districts, Ciudad de la Paz and Mbere.[5] The capital is Ciudad de la Paz ("City of Peace"),[7] known as Oyala until 2017.[8] In the 2017 national parliamentary election, Djibloho elected one senator and one deputy.[9]

<title>Nursultan</title>
<content>
**Nursultan** (Template:Lang-kk, Template:IPA-kk) is a Kazakh male name. *Nur sultan* can be literally translated as "radiant sultan", "the sultan of sunlight" in the Kazakh language.


**Nur-Sultan** (Template:Lang-kk) was the name of the capital of Kazakhstan from 2019 to 2022, the city is currently known as Astana. The name was given to the capital when it was named after Nursultan Nazarbayev.


**Nursultan** may refer to:



* Nursultan Nazarbayev (born 1940), president of Kazakhstan from 1990 to 2019, who the capital city was named for from 2019 to 2022
* Nursultan Belgibayev (born 1991), Kazakhstani ice hockey player
* Nursultan Mamayev (born 1993), Kazakhstani taekwondo practitioner
* Nursultan Bimurza (born 1994), Kazakhstani volleyball player
* Nursultan Nazarbayev International Airport, Kazakhstan's second busiest airport

**Islamabad** (/ɪzˈlɑːməbæd/;[7] Template:Lang-ur, listenⓘ; transl. 'City of Islam') is the capital city of Pakistan.[8] It is the country's ninth-most populous city with a population of over 1.2 million people[9] and is federally administered by the Pakistani government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s, it replaced Karachi as Pakistan's official national capital. The city is notable for its high standards of living,[10] safety,[11] cleanliness, abundant greenery and architecture.[12]

<document>
<title>Vatican City</title>
<fragment>
In statistics comparing countries in various per capita or per area metrics, Vatican City is often an outlier—these can stem from the state's small size and ecclesiastical function.[121] For example, as most of the roles which would confer citizenship are reserved for men, the gender ratio of the citizenship is several men per woman.[122] Further oddities are petty crimes against tourists resulting in a very high per-capita crime rate,[123] and the city-state leading the world in per-capita wine consumption due to its sacramental use.[121] A jocular illustration of these anomalies is sometimes made by calculating a "Popes per km2" statistic, which is greater than two because the country is less than half a square kilometre in area.[124]




</fragment>

msg.content:
Based on my search of Wikipedia, here are some of the most densely populated capital cities and city-states by population density:

## **Densely Populated Capitals & City-States**

### **Highest Density by City Proper:**
From the "List of cities proper by population density":

1. **Manila, Philippines** - Approximately 43,064 people/km² (111,537 per sq mi)
2. **Mandaluyong, Philippines** - 38,495 people/km² (99,703 per sq mi) 
3. **Pateros, Philippines** - 37,061 people/km² (95,988 per sq mi)
4. **Caloocan, Philippines** - 31,233 people/km² (80,893 per sq mi)
5. **Bnei Brak, Israel** - 30,854 people/km² (79,911 per sq mi)
6. **Kathmandu, Nepal** - 29,161 people/km² (75,526 per sq mi)
7. **Dhaka, Bangladesh** - 29,069 people/km² (75,289 per sq mi)

### **City-States:**
While not appearing in the main list, these city-states have extremely high densities:

- **Vatican City** - 1,559 people/km² (4,037 per sq mi)
- **Singapore** - As a city-state, has the highest population density among countries
- **Monaco** - Also extremely dense as a city-state

### **Key Observations:**

1. **Philippine cities dominate** the top spots, with multiple Metro Manila cities having densities over 30,000 people/km²
2. **Manila** stands out as the most densely populated capital city proper globally
3. The list focuses on **city proper boundaries**, not metropolitan areas
4. **Geography matters** - many of these cities are landlocked or have limited expansion options

The data shows that Southeast Asian cities, particularly in the Philippines, have some of the highest population densities among capital cities worldwide when measured by city proper boundaries.

<title>Tel Aviv</title>
<fragment>
1. **^** West and East Jerusalem combined have 901,000 residents, more than twice as many as Tel Aviv-Yafo with 444,000. West Jerusalem alone has a population of 348,000.[8]
2. **^** Jerusalem is Israel's capital according to the Jerusalem Law passed in 1980. The presidential residence, government offices, supreme court and parliament (Knesset) are located there. The Palestinian Authority foresees East Jerusalem as the capital of its future state. The UN does not recognize Jerusalem as Israel's capital, taking the position that the final status of Jerusalem is pending future negotiations between Israel and the Palestinian Authorities.[9] Countries maintain their embassies in Tel Aviv and its suburbs, or suburbs of Jerusalem, such as Mevaseret Zion.[10] Czech Republic, Guatemala, Honduras, Taiwan, the United States, and Vanuatu recognize Jerusalem as the capital of Israel.

This is a **list of cities worldwide by population density**. <document>
<title>Mumbai</title>
<fragment>

Mumbai suffers from the same major urbanization problems seen in many fast growing cities in developing countries: poverty and unemployment. With available land at a premium, Mumbai residents often reside in cramped, relatively expensive housing, usually far from workplaces, and therefore requiring long commutes on crowded mass transit, or clogged roadways. Many of them live close to bus or train stations, although suburban residents spend significant time travelling southward to the main commercial district.[332] Dharavi, Asia's second largest slum (if Karachi's Orangi Town is counted as a single slum)[333] is located in central Mumbai and houses between 800,000 and 10 lakh (one million) people[334] in 2.39 km2 (0.92 sq mi), making it one of the most densely populated areas on Earth[335] with a population density of at least 334,728 persons per square kilometre.[336]


</fragment>
<fragment>

| Data is based on Government of India Census.Source: MMRDA[326] |


![](image)Shri Siddhivinayak Temple is one of the most popular Hindu temples in the city.
According to the 2011 census, the population of Mumbai city was 12,479,608. The population density is estimated to be about 20,482 persons per square kilometre. The living space is 4.5 square metres per person.[327] Mumbai Metropolitan Region was home to 20,748,395 people by 2011.[10] Greater Mumbai, the area under the administration of the MCGM, has a literacy rate of 94.7%, higher than the national average of 86.7%. The number of slum-dwellers in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region is estimated to be 90 lakh (9 million), up from 60 lakh (6 million) in 2001 which constitutes approximately 38.5% of the region.[328][329]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)
Some of the tallest skyscrapers of Mumbai, like World One and Lodha Park complexes, can be found in Lower Parel.
![](image)
Antilia and Lodha Altamount skyscrapers on Altamount Road, also known as India's Billionaires' Row.

Mumbai is India's largest city (by population) and is the financial and commercial capital of the country as it generates 6.16% of the total GDP.[32][146][199] It serves as an economic hub of India; as of 2006, Mumbai contributed 10% of the nation's factory employment, 25% of industrial output, 33% of income tax collections, 60% of customs duty collections, 20% of central excise tax collections, 40% of foreign trade, and ₹40 billion (equivalent to ₹130 billion or US$1.5 billion in 2023) in corporate taxes.[200]

[edit]

Under French law, people born in foreign countries with no French citizenship at birth are defined as immigrants. According to the 2012 census, 135,853 residents of the City of Paris were immigrants from Europe, 112,369 were immigrants from the Maghreb, 70,852 from sub-Saharan Africa and Egypt, 5,059 from Turkey, 91,297 from Asia (outside Turkey), 38,858 from the Americas, and 1,365 from the South Pacific.[167]

According to INSEE, the population has dropped by 122,919, or about five percent, over the past decade. The Mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, declared that this illustrated the "de-densification" of the city, creating more green space and less crowding.[153][154] Despite the drop, Paris remains the most densely-populated city in Europe, with 252 residents per hectare, not counting parks.[155] This drop was attributed partly to a lower birth rate, the departure of middle-class residents and the possible loss of housing in the city due to short-term rentals for tourism.[156]

![](image)Dharavi compared to other great slums in the world. Map according to Mike Davis.
**Dharavi** is a residential area in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India. It has often been considered to be one of the world's largest slums.[1][2] Dharavi has an area of just over 2.39 square kilometres (0.92 sq mi; 590 acres)[3] and a population of about 1,000,000. With a population density of over 277,136/km2 (717,780/sq mi), Dharavi is one of the most densely populated areas in the world.


The Dharavi slum was founded in 1884 during the British colonial era, and grew because the expulsion of factories and residents from the peninsular city centre by the colonial government and from the migration of rural Indians into urban Mumbai. For this reason, Dharavi is currently a highly diverse settlement religiously and ethnically.[4]


</fragment>

By the late 20th century, Dharavi occupied about 175 hectares (432 acres), with an astounding population density of more than 2,900 people per hectare (1,200/acre).[12][14]

[edit]

![](image)A traditional pottery unit in Dharavi.
![](image)Street vendors and farmers market along the road passing through Dharavi slum in Mumbai.
There have been many plans since 1997 to redevelop Dharavi like the former slums of Hong Kong such as Tai Hang. In 2004, the cost of redevelopment was estimated to be ₹5,000 crore (US$590 million).[15] Companies from around the world have bid to redevelop Dharavi,[16] including Lehman Brothers, Dubai's Limitless and Singapore's Capitaland Ltd.[16] In 2010, it was estimated to cost ₹15,000 crore (US$1.8 billion) to redevelop.[15]

**Islamabad** (/ɪzˈlɑːməbæd/;[7] Template:Lang-ur, listenⓘ; transl. 'City of Islam') is the capital city of Pakistan.[8] It is the country's ninth-most populous city with a population of over 1.2 million people[9] and is federally administered by the Pakistani government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s, it replaced Karachi as Pakistan's official national capital. The city is notable for its high standards of living,[10] safety,[11] cleanliness, abundant greenery and architecture.[12]

Expanding the town area has – apart from financial restrictions – proven to be challenging due to its geographical location. In southern, eastern and western directions, Windhoek is surrounded by rocky, mountainous areas, which make land development costly. The southern side is not suitable for industrial development because of the presence of underground aquifers. This leaves the vast Brakwater area north of town the only feasible place for Windhoek's expansion.[26]


Windhoek's city council has plans to dramatically expand the city's boundaries such that the town area will cover 5,133.4 km2 (1,982.0 sq mi). Windhoek would become the third-largest city in the world by area,[*citation needed*] after Tianjin and Istanbul, although its population density is only 63 inhabitants per square kilometre.[27]

Based on my research from Wikipedia, here are some major capital cities that were **purpose-built/specially planned** to serve as their nation's capital:

## Established Planned Capitals

### **Abuja, Nigeria**
- **Planned:** 1976, officially became capital in 1991
- **Why:** Replaced Lagos as capital to alleviate overcrowding and provide a more centrally located, neutral territory for the federal government
- **Features:** Designed as a modern, well-organized city in the center of Nigeria

### **Canberra, Australia**
- **Planned:** Early 1900s, capital since 1913
- **Why:** Chosen as compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne after Australia's federation
- **Features:** Garden city design, planned with lakes, parks, and geometric street patterns

### **Islamabad, Pakistan**
- **Planned:** 1960s, completed move from Karachi by 1966
- **Why:** To diversify development rather than concentrating everything in coastal Karachi
- **Features:** Modern planned city with organized sectors and green spaces

### **Windhoek, Namibia**
- **Planned:** German colonial planning in late 1800s/early 1900s
- **Features:** Designed with a unique layout in a mountainous setting

### **Gaborone, Botswana**
- **Built:** 1964, became capital at independence
- **Why:** Replaced Mahikeng (in South Africa) as capital when Botswana gained independence

### **Dhaka, Bangladesh**
- **Purpose-built aspects:** While ancient, it was extensively planned and developed as capital when Bangladesh gained independence in 1971

## Currently Under Construction

- **New Administrative Capital, Egypt** (replacing Cairo partially)
- **Djibloho, Equatorial Guinea** (replacing Malabo)
- **New Clark City, Philippines** (planned completion by 2030)

These cities were chosen and built specifically as capitals rather than evolving naturally into that role, allowing for planned infrastructure, governance facilities, and urban design from the ground up.

**Islamabad** (/ɪzˈlɑːməbæd/;[7] Template:Lang-ur, listenⓘ; transl. 'City of Islam') is the capital city of Pakistan.[8] It is the country's ninth-most populous city with a population of over 1.2 million people[9] and is federally administered by the Pakistani government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. <title>Canberra Plan</title>
<content>
For the urban plan of the city of Canberra, Australia, see Canberra § Urban structure.

In philosophy, the **Canberra Plan** is a contemporary program of methodology and analysis that answers questions about what the world is like according to physics.[1] It is considered a naturalistic approach in metaphysics, which holds that metaphysics can explain the features of the world described by physics and what the different classes of everyday belief represent.[1] A more detailed description of the plan refers to it as a family of doctrines that are grounded on a physicalist worldview as well as a priori philosophizing to explain our thoughts about our world as revealed by physics.[2]


The Canberra Plan arose in the 1990s at the Australian National University in Canberra, Australia. Its originators were David Lewis and Frank Jackson. An important question that it raises concerns what to say once "it turns out that there is nothing of which the a priori theory is true."[2]


There are those who say that the Canberra Plan could prove insufficient and inconsistent to effectively pick out a feature of or relationship in the world.[3]

Behind the construction of Brasília lay a monumental campaign to construct an entire city in the barren center of the country,[37] hundreds of kilometers from any major city. The brainchild of Kubitschek, Niemeyer had as aims included stimulating industry, integrating the country's distant areas, populating inhospitable regions and bringing progress to a region where only cattle ranching then existed. Niemeyer and Costa used it to test new concepts of city planning: streets without transit, buildings floating off the ground supported by columns and allowing the space underneath to be free and integrated with nature.

Following the opening of Brasilia, the modern design attracted the interest of artists, theater and musical groups, and younger generations of Brazilian citizens. One reason for this particular crowd was a coordinated effort to make Brasilia the new cultural center of the country. There were venues during the city's first years to help encourage artistic activities, such as the International Congress of Art Critics in 1959, an annual National Salon for several years in the early 1960s, and the establishment of several musical and theatrical groups.[22]


Since its initial completion, Brasilia has gone through several stages of population changes. After initial interest following the opening, population numbers decreased before recovering in the late 1960s. Brasilia is now estimated to be Brazil's 3rd most populous city.

**Islamabad** (/ɪzˈlɑːməbæd/;[7] Template:Lang-ur, listenⓘ; transl. 'City of Islam') is the capital city of Pakistan.[8] It is the country's ninth-most populous city with a population of over 1.2 million people[9] and is federally administered by the Pakistani government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s, it replaced Karachi as Pakistan's official national capital. **Islamabad** (/ɪzˈlɑːməbæd/;[7] Template:Lang-ur, listenⓘ; transl. 'City of Islam') is the capital city of Pakistan.[8] It is the country's ninth-most populous city with a population of over 1.2 million people[9] and is federally administered by the Pakistani government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s, it replaced Karachi as Pakistan's official national capital. The city is notable for its high standards of living,[10] safety,[11] cleanliness, abundant greenery and architecture.[12]

<title>History of Ankara</title>
<fragment>
![](image)The historic Ankara Palas Hotel (1927).
Ankara is one of the world's oldest capital cities, having been a major urban center, though not a capital, for far longer than cities like London, Paris or Madrid; even Istanbul. When present Istanbul, then the Roman provincial town of Byzantium, was being groomed as a new capital for the Roman Empire in 324, Ankara was already an important administrative center from which most of the northern half of what is now Turkey was run.[2]

The **history of Ankara** can be traced back to the Bronze Age Hatti civilization, which was succeeded in the 2nd millennium BC by the Hittites, in the 10th century BC by the Phrygians, and later by the Lydians, Persians, Macedonians, Galatians, Romans, Byzantines, Seljuks, and Ottomans.




## Hatti, Hittite and Phrygian periods

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)The historic Ziraat Bank Building (1929).
After Ankara became the capital of the newly founded Republic of Turkey, new development divided the city into an old section, called **Ulus**, and a new section, called **Yenişehir**. Ancient buildings reflecting Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman history and narrow winding streets mark the old section. The new section, now centered around **Kızılay**, has the trappings of a more modern city: wide streets, hotels, theaters, shopping malls, and high-rises. Government offices and foreign embassies are also located in the new section.

The **history of Ottawa**, capital of Canada, was shaped by events such as the construction of the Rideau Canal, the lumber industry, the choice of Ottawa as the location of Canada's capital, as well as American and European influences and interactions. By 1914, Ottawa's population had surpassed 100,000 and today it is the capital of a G7 country whose metropolitan population exceeds one million.


The origin of the name "Ottawa" is derived from the Algonquin word *adawe*, meaning "to trade". The word refers to the indigenous peoples who used the river to trade, hunt, fish, camp, harvest plants, ceremonies, and for other traditional uses. The first maps made of the area started to name the major river after these peoples.

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, here's a comparison of how several national capitals were selected and planned, including their unique challenges and design philosophies:

## **Canberra, Australia**

**Why it was built:** Following Australian federation in 1901, the new nation needed a capital that wouldn't favor either Sydney or Melbourne, the two largest cities competing for the privilege.

**Planning process:**
- Capital location chosen in 1908 as a compromise - neutral territory between Sydney and Melbourne
- International design competition held in 1911, won by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin
- Design emphasized garden city principles with geometric patterns radiating from hills
- Construction began in 1913, but development was slow due to World War I and the Great Depression
- Griffin's vision was partially implemented but faced numerous modifications over time

**Unique challenge:** Creating a national identity for a brand new country while balancing competing regional interests.

## **Ottawa, Canada**

**Why it was chosen:** Selected by Queen Victoria in 1857 as a compromise between competing claims of Toronto, Montreal, Quebec City, and Kingston.

**Planning characteristics:**
- Not originally purpose-built - grew from existing settlement
- Chosen for strategic location: defensible position on Ottawa River, bilingual community, distance from US border
- Capital functions gradually added to existing town rather than comprehensive pre-planning
- Government buildings clustered around Parliament Hill
- Later planning initiatives like the Greber Plan (1950s) attempted to create more cohesive capital design

**Unique challenge:** Integrating capital functions into an existing city while accommodating Canada's bilingual nature and regional tensions.

## **Brasília, Brazil**

**Why it was built:** Part of President Juscelino Kubitschek's modernization vision ("fifty years of progress in five"), moving capital from Rio de Janeiro to develop Brazil's interior.

**Planning process:**
- Entirely purpose-built on undeveloped savanna
- Designed by urban planner Lúcio Costa and architect Oscar Niemeyer (1956-1960)
- Built in remarkable 41-month timeframe
- Modernist design with airplane-shaped layout and monumental architecture
- Intended to symbolize Brazil's emergence as a modern nation

**Unique challenge:** Building a modern capital from scratch in remote interior to drive national development and break from colonial past.

## **New Delhi, India**

**Why it was built:** The British decided to move India's capital from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911 to be closer to the heartland and create a more imposing imperial presence.

**Planning process:**
- Designed by British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker
- Built adjacent to existing Delhi (the "old city" of Shahjahanabad)
- Construction from 1912-1931
- Imperial grandeur with wide boulevards, monumental architecture, and deliberate symbolism
- Incorporated elements of Indian architecture while maintaining British imperial aesthetics

**Unique challenge:** Creating a capital that projected British imperial power while acknowledging India's cultural heritage.

## **Key Differences in Planning Approaches:**

**Canberra** - International competition, garden city ideals, slow organic growth despite master plan
**Ottawa** - Evolutionary approach, capital functions added to existing settlement
**Brasília** - Rapid construction, modernist utopian vision, completely purpose-built
**New Delhi** - Imperial grandeur, built beside historic city, blend of Western and indigenous elements

## **Common Challenges:**

1. **Political compromise** - All involved balancing competing regional or political interests
2. **National identity** - Each capital meant to symbolize the nation's aspirations
3. **Implementation gaps** - Master plans often modified by practical, political, or financial constraints
4. **Cultural integration** - Creating spaces that work for diverse populations
5. **Future growth** - Planning for expansion beyond original visions

The most successful capitals tended to balance ambitious visionary planning with practical considerations of existing conditions, cultural contexts, and political realities.

**Islamabad** (/ɪzˈlɑːməbæd/;[7] Template:Lang-ur, listenⓘ; transl. 'City of Islam') is the capital city of Pakistan.[8] It is the country's ninth-most populous city with a population of over 1.2 million people[9] and is federally administered by the Pakistani government as part of the Islamabad Capital Territory. Built as a planned city in the 1960s, it replaced Karachi as Pakistan's official national capital. The city is notable for its high standards of living,[10] safety,[11] cleanliness, abundant greenery and architecture.[12]

The current **capital of Brazil**, since its construction in 1960, is Brasilia. Rio de Janeiro was the country's capital between 1763 and 1960. The city of Salvador served as the seat for the Portuguese colonial administration in Brazil for its first two centuries and is usually called the "first capital of Brazil."



## History

[edit]


</fragment>

In the 1950s plans were considered for moving the federal capital from the east coast to the interior; the interior was sparsely populated and it was hoped that moving the capital to the region would help populate the area. The new capital, Brasília, was inaugurated as the federal capital on 21 April 1960 after being purpose built for $2 trillion U.S.

# Planned Capitals: Purpose-Built Seats of Government and Global Influence

Based on my research of planned capital cities around the world, I can provide a comprehensive overview of how these purpose-built seats of government influence global perspectives on urban development, governance, and national identity.

## The Three Major Planned Capitals

### **Washington, D.C. - The Modern Prototype**
Washington, D.C. represents the most influential example of a purpose-built national capital in the modern era. Established through the Residence Act of 1790, it was created specifically to serve as the federal capital of the United States, separate from any existing state to ensure political neutrality.

**Key Features:**
- **Planner**: Pierre Charles L'Enfant created the original plan featuring broad avenues, ceremonial spaces, and a systematic grid pattern
- **Design Philosophy**: Embodied Enlightenment ideals of order, democracy, and civic virtue
- **Global Impact**: Set the precedent for capital city planning worldwide, influencing how governments express national values through urban design
- **Symbolic Elements**: The Capitol Building, White House, andNational Mall create a powerful narrative about American democracy

### **Brasília - The Modernist Vision**
Brasília stands as perhaps the most ambitious planned capital project of the 20th century. Built between 1956-1960, it represents Brazil's bold vision for modernization and national unity.

**Key Features:**
- **Planners**: Lúcio Costa (urban planning) and Oscar Niemeyer (architecture) led the groundbreaking design team
- **Design Philosophy**: Modernist architecture and urban planning principles, with the city shaped like an airplane or bird
- **Construction**: Inaugurated on April 21, 1960, at the cost of $2 trillion U.S. (historical value)
- **Architectural Significance**: Features iconic structures like the Brazilian National Congress, Cathedral of Brasília, and Palácio do Planalto
- **Global Recognition**: UNESCO World Heritage Site, celebrated as a masterpiece of modernist urban planning

### **Abuja - The African Model**
Nigeria's purpose-built capital Abuja officially became the seat of government in 1991, moving from the coastal city of Lagos to a more central location.

**Key Features:**
- **Rationale**: Geographic centrality, ethnic neutrality, and relief from overcrowding in Lagos
- **Federal Capital Territory**: Establishes a special administrative district similar to Washington, D.C.
- **Development Purpose**: Intended to stimulate development of Nigeria's interior regions

## Global Impact and Influence

### **Political Symbolism**
Planned capitals serve as powerful symbols of national identity:
- **Neutrality**: By creating new capitals away from existing major cities, governments emphasize fairness and national unity over regional dominance
- **Modernization**: These cities project forward-looking national aspirations and break with colonial or historical associations

### **Urban Planning Innovation**
Each capital pioneered different urban planning concepts:
- **Washington, D.C.**: Integration of ceremonial spaces with practical governance, use of monumental axes
- **Brasília**: Modernist planning principles, separation of traffic circulation, emphasis on architectural harmony
- **Abuja**: Adaptation of planning principles to tropical African context and multi-ethnic nation-building

### **Architectural Legacy**
These capitals have influenced global architecture:
- **Neoclassical Elements** (Washington) spread worldwide as symbols of democracy
- **Modernist Architecture** (Brasília) influenced global design trends, particularly for institutional buildings
- **Cultural Synthesis** (Abuja) demonstrates how planned capitals can incorporate local cultural elements

### **Governance Models**
The creation of special federal territories (like the District of Columbia and Federal Capital Territory) provided models for:
- Administrative autonomy for capital cities
- Balancing local governance with national interests
- Urban management of politically sensitive areas

## Challenges and Adaptations

### **Economic Viability**
- High construction and maintenance costs
- Need to create complete urban ecosystems from scratch
- Ongoing development challenges as cities grow

### **Cultural Criticism**
- Some planned capitals criticized for lacking organic growth and cultural authenticity
- Brasília initially faced criticism for being too modernist and disconnected from Brazilian urban traditions
- Washington, D.C. evolved significantly from its original plan to accommodate organic growth

### **Social Dynamics**
- Creating social cohesion in artificially created urban environments
- Addressing housing for diverse populations
- Balancing ceremonial spaces with everyday life needs

## Contemporary Relevance

Today's planned capitals continue to influence:
1. **New Nation Planning**: Countries establishing themselves often consider purpose-built capitals
2. **Administrative Reform**: Some nations contemplate capital relocation for strategic reasons
3. **Sustainable Development**: Modern planned capitals increasingly incorporate environmental considerations
4. **Smart City Concepts**: New administrative capitals often serve as laboratories for urban innovation

The planned capital model represents a unique approach to expressing national values through urban design, where every street, building, and public space contributes to a larger narrative about governance, identity, and aspiration. These cities remain powerful case studies in how architecture and planning can shape political culture and international perceptions.

Based on my research, here's information about famous planned cities that became capital cities:

## Major Planned Capital Cities

### 1. **Brasília, Brazil** 🇧🇷
- **Construction period**: Built 1956-1960
- **Inaugurated**: April 21, 1960
- **Moved from**: Rio de Janeiro
- **Purpose**: To develop Brazil's interior and create a more centrally located capital
- **Designers**: Lucio Costa (urban planner) and Oscar Niemeyer (architect)
- **Notable features**: 
  - airplane-shaped layout
  - modernist architecture with concrete structures
  - UNESCO World Heritage Site
  - Landmark Cathedral of Brasília and National Congress buildings

### 2. **Abuja, Nigeria** 🇳🇬
- **Construction period**: Built 1976-1991
- **Officially became capital**: December 12, 1991
- **Moved from**: Lagos
- **Purpose**: To create a more neutral, centrally located capital away from ethnic tensions in Lagos
- **Designer**: International team led by Japanese architect Kenzo Tange
- **Notable features**: Master-planned city with districts, Aso Rock presidential complex

### 3. **Canberra, Australia** 🇦🇺
- **Construction period**: Built 1913-1927
- **Officially became capital**: 1927 (parliament moved from Melbourne)
- **Chosen as capital**: Compromise between Sydney and Melbourne rivalry
- **Designers**: Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin (American architects)
- **Notable features**: Garden city design, geometric layout with circles and triangles, Lake Burley Griffin

### 4. **Islamabad, Pakistan** 🇵🇰
- **Construction period**: Built 1960s
- **Officially became capital**: 1966
- **Moved from**: Karachi
- **Purpose**: More centrally located, better climate, and government security
- **Designer**: Greek architect Konstantinos Apostolos Doxiadis
- **Notable features**: Modern grid layout, Margalla Hills backdrop, organized sectors

### 5. **Washington, D.C., USA** 🇺🇸
- **Construction period**: Founded 1790, formally established 1800
- **Designer**: Pierre L'Enfant (French-American architect)
- **Purpose**: To create a national capital independent of any state
- **Notable features**: Monumental layout with Pennsylvania Avenue, National Mall, Capitol building

These cities share common characteristics:
- Built specifically to serve as national capitals
- Designed from scratch rather than growing organically
- Often created to solve political or geographical problems
- Feature significant architectural and urban planning innovations
- Include monumental government buildings and symbolic spaces

Each represents different eras of urban planning philosophy, from L'Enfant's 18th-century baroque design for Washington to the modernist symbolism of Brasília.

<title>Juscelino Kubitschek</title>
<fragment>

The construction of Brasilia fostered the development of many roads, linking Brazil's vast territories. One important example was the construction of the Belém-Brasilia road. Previously, the only way to go from Rio or São Paulo to Belém was via ship on the Atlantic Ocean. During the Second World War, this weak link had been blocked by German U-boats, virtually disrupting all commerce.



![](image)Monument to Kubitschek and his wife Sarah in front of the JK Memorial.
The new capital was soon to help integrate all the Brazilian regions, create jobs and absorb a workforce from the Brazilian Northeast, and to stimulate the economy of the Central-west and North. During the construction of Brasilia, in the haste to finish the job, accidents were frequent, something Kubitschek's government did its utmost to cover up.[13]



### Corruption

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The work, led by urban planner Lúcio Costa, architect Oscar Niemeyer and landscape designer Roberto Burle Marx, started in February 1957. More than 200 machines were put to work and 30,000 workers came from every part of the country, though most from the northeast. The construction went on day and night to meet the objective of finishing Brasília by 21 April 1960, in a homage to the Inconfidência Mineira and Rome's founding. A completely new capital city, its streets, government palaces, infrastructure, living facilities, etc., suddenly emerged in the middle of a savanna in just 41 months, and before the target date. As soon as it was inaugurated, Brasília was considered a masterpiece of urbanism and modern architecture.


Brasilia plays a strategic role in integrating Brazil's farthest regions, bringing development to unpopulated areas and guaranteeing Brazil's cultural and territorial unity.

The **Federal Capital Territory** (**FCT**) is a federal territory in central Nigeria. Abuja, the capital city of Nigeria, is located in this territory. The FCT was formed in 1976[4] from parts of the states of old Kaduna, Kwara, Niger, and Plateau states, with the bulk of land mass carved out of Niger state. The Federal Capital Territory is within the North Central region of the country. Unlike other states of Nigeria, which are headed by elected Governors, it is administered by the Federal Capital Territory Administration, headed by a minister, who is appointed by the president.[5]

## Man and Capital: 19-20世纪的四代人建都故事

人类历史上，首都迁移和新建往往标志着国家发展的重大转折。通过分析四个不同时期的人类活动——1790年的美国、1950年代的巴西、20世纪末的尼日利亚，以及20世纪初的澳大利亚——我们可以看到四代人跨越三个世纪的建都壮举，每个都承载着独特的时代使命和国家愿景。

---

### **第一代（18世纪）：理性的建国者（华盛顿特区，1790年）**

1790年7月16日，美国国会通过了著名的《居住法案》（Residence Act），这是对新生国家政治焦虑的理性回应。当时美国建国不过十余年，各州之间南北矛盾激烈，在首都选址上争论不休。北方的商业州希望首都在经济发达的波士顿或费城，而南方的农业州则倾向于位置更南的地点。

这种政治分歧的背后，是新生国家对权力平衡的深切忧虑。最终，通过政治妥协，选择了位于马里兰州和弗吉尼亚州之间的波托马克河畔作为新首都所在地。1791年，乔治·华盛顿总统亲自勘定了这片约100平方英里的土地，并将其命名为"哥伦比亚特区"，以纪念发现新大陆的哥伦布。

**第一代建都者的特征**：
- **理性妥协**：通过政治协商解决区域分歧
- **战略考量**：选址考虑国家地理中心和南北平衡
- **渐进发展**：不是一夜之间的搬迁，而是逐步建设
- **理想主义**：体现民主共和理念，强调联邦统一

---

### **第二代（20世纪初期）：现代化的梦想家（巴西利亚，1956-1960年）**

20世纪中期，巴西总统尤塞利诺·库比契克（Juscelino Kubitschek）提出了一个雄心勃勃的建都计划，这在巴西1927年就写入了宪法，但一直未能实施。库比契克的口号是"五十年腾飞"，他要在巴西利亚项目上证明巴西从殖民地国家向现代化强国的跨越。

1956年2月，库比契克任命城市规划师卢西奥·科斯塔（Lúcio Costa）负责总体规划，建筑师奥斯卡·尼迈耶（Oscar Niemeyer）设计所有公共建筑，景观设计师罗伯托·布雷尔·马克斯负责绿化设计。这座新首都的建设创造了建筑史上的奇迹：

**建设数据**：
- **建设周期**：41个月（1957年2月开工，1960年4月21日落成）
- **人力动员**：来自巴西各地约30,000名工人，多数来自东北部
- **机械投入**：200多台机器24小时作业
- **地理位置**：选在巴西地理中心附近，从无到有建在热带稀树草原上

库比契克的建都不仅是一个建筑工程项目，更是国家重建的象征。新首都很快发挥了重要作用：
- 连接巴西广袤领土的交通网络得到发展
- 创造就业机会，吸收东北部劳动力
- 激励中西部和北部经济发展
- 再次确认巴西的文化和领土统一

**第二代建都者的特征**：
- **现代化雄心**：追求工业化和国家现代化
- **快速建设**：体现效率主义和"发展主义"理念
- **国家整合**：通过首都建设促进领土统一和地区平衡
- **文化自信**：用现代建筑语言表达拉丁美洲的独立精神

---

### **第三代（20世纪后期）：国家整合的追求者（阿布贾，1976年至今）**

尼日利亚的迁都进程始于1976年，当时该国刚刚经历内战结束7年。军事政府的穆尔塔拉·穆罕默德将军决定将首都从沿海的大城市拉各斯迁往内陆中心地带的阿布贾。这一决定背后的逻辑是：

**迁都背景和动机**：
- **政治平衡**：拉各斯位于南方基督教区，政府希望平衡北方穆斯林地区
- **国家统一**：内战创伤需要通过地理中心的首都来强化国家认同
- **战略安全**：沿海城市在冷战中面临安全风险
- **分散发展**：避免过度集中在沿海地区

阿布贾的建设是一代人的长期工程：
- **1976年**：联邦首都特区成立，从几个州划拨土地
- **1980年代**：基础设施建设和政府机构搬迁开始
- **1991年12月12日**：阿布贾正式成为尼日利亚首都

建设遇到了诸多挑战，包括资金不足、管理问题、生活方式转型的困难等，但最终实现了国家的战略目标。

**第三代建都者的特征**：
- **民族和解**：通过迁都修复内战创伤和地区矛盾
- **战略深度**：从沿海向内陆转移，增强国家战略安全
- **渐进坚持**：几代人的长期努力，不为短期困难所挫
- **包容发展**：试图融合不同地区、宗教、族群的国家认同

---

### **第四代（20世纪前期）：殖民遗产的继承者（堪培拉，1911年至今）**

澳大利亚的故事有所不同。作为英国殖民地，澳大利亚在1901年联邦化后立即面临首都选址问题。悉尼和墨尔本这两个最大城市之间的竞争，体现了殖民时期留下的城市发展矛盾。

**堪培拉的诞生过程**：
- **1901年**：澳大利亚联邦成立，首都问题成为政治争论焦点
- **1908年**：悉尼和墨尔本妥协，选择内陆建新都，同时墨尔本作为临时首都
- **1911年**：举办国际设计竞赛，美国建筑师沃尔特·伯利·格里芬中标
- **1913年**：奠基仪式，命名为"堪培拉"

堪培拉的发展虽然不如巴西利亚那样迅速，但体现了另一代建都者的智慧：
- **文化传承**：在城市设计中融合澳大利亚原住民文化元素
- **民主理念**：规划中强调公共服务和民主参与的场所设计
- **生态意识**：早期就注重环境保护和可持续发展
- **国际视野**：通过国际竞赛接受全球智慧

堪培拉的建设体现了一种更加稳健、持续的建都模式，其发展贯穿了整个20世纪。

**第四代建都者的特征**：
- **文化融合**：融合英式民主传统和澳大利亚本土文化
- **渐进务实**：不求一时之功，而是持续建设发展
- **国际开放**：通过国际竞赛引入全球智慧
- **生态先锋**：在规划中体现环境保护和可持续理念

---

### **共同的使命与世代的差异**

通过这四次建都故事，我们可以看到建都活动从第一代到第四代呈现出的鲜明轨迹：

**时代精神的演变**：
1. **理性启蒙时代**（华盛顿特区）：强调政治理性和制度设计
2. **发展主义时代**（巴西利亚）：追求快速现代化和国家崛起
3. **民族和解时代**（阿布贾）：注重国家统一和包容发展
4. **文化自觉时代**（堪培拉）：融合传统文化与现代治理

**建设方式的差异**：
- **速度**：从渐进建设（华盛顿）到急速建设（巴西利亚），再回到平衡发展（阿布贾、堪培拉）
- **技术**：从手工建设到机械化施工，再到高新技术应用
- **理念**：从政治稳定到经济发展，再到文化传承和生态保护

但无论时代如何变迁，建都活动始终是人类文明中最具象征性的国家行为之一。每一代建都者都在回应自己时代的核心问题，同时也在为后世留下超越时空的遗产。

---

### **启示与当代意义**

在21世纪的今天，随着全球化和气候变化等新挑战的出现，首都建设将面临新的使命：

**当代迁都的新趋势**：
- **气候适应**：应对海平面上升、极端天气等气候变化挑战
- **数字整合**：适应数字经济和远程办公的新模式
- **城市韧性**：提高首都面对突发事件的抗风险能力
- **文化多样**：在全球化背景下保护和弘扬本土文化

这四个跨越三个世纪的建都故事告诉我们，首都建设不仅是建筑工程，更是国家愿景的物化表达。每一代建都者都在用自己的方式回应时代的核心问题，创造属于自己时代的精神丰碑。无论是18世纪的理性建国者，20世纪的现代化梦想家，还是追求国家整合的政治家，他们共同谱写了人类建都史上最壮美的篇章。

这些经验对于今天面临城市化和国家治理挑战的发展中国家来说，依然具有重要的参考价值。在快速的城市化进程中，如何在现代建设与传统保护之间找到平衡，如何在发展速度与质量之间做出取舍，如何让首都真正成为全体人民的国家认同象征——这些问题都值得我们思考和实践。

## Man and Capital: 19-20世纪的四代人建都故事

人类历史上，首都迁移和新建往往标志着国家发展的重大转折。通过分析四个不同时期的人类活动——1790年的美国、1950年代的巴西、20世纪末的尼日利亚，以及20世纪初的澳大利亚——我们可以看到四代人跨越三个世纪的建都壮举，每个都承载着独特的时代使命和国家愿景。

---

### **第一代（18世纪）：理性的建国者（华盛顿特区，1790年）**

1790年7月16日，美国国会通过了著名的《居住法案》（Residence Act），这是对新生国家政治焦虑的理性回应。当时美国建国不过十余年，各州之间南北矛盾激烈，在首都选址上争论不休。北方的商业州希望首都在经济发达的波士顿或费城，而南方的农业州则倾向于位置更南的地点。

这种政治分歧的背后，是新生国家对权力平衡的深切忧虑。最终，通过政治妥协，选择了位于马里兰州和弗吉尼亚州之间的波托马克河畔作为新首都所在地。1791年，乔治·华盛顿总统亲自勘定了这片约100平方英里的土地，并将其命名为"哥伦比亚特区"，以纪念发现新大陆的哥伦布。

**第一代建都者的特征**：
- **理性妥协**：通过政治协商解决区域分歧
- **战略考量**：选址考虑国家地理中心和南北平衡
- **渐进发展**：不是一夜之间的搬迁，而是逐步建设
- **理想主义**：体现民主共和理念，强调联邦统一

---

### **第二代（20世纪初期）：现代化的梦想家（巴西利亚，1956-1960年）**

20世纪中期，巴西总统尤塞利诺·库比契克（Juscelino Kubitschek）提出了一个雄心勃勃的建都计划，这在巴西1927年就写入了宪法，但一直未能实施。库比契克的口号是"五十年腾飞"，他要在巴西利亚项目上证明巴西从殖民地国家向现代化强国的跨越。

1956年2月，库比契克任命城市规划师卢西奥·科斯塔（Lúcio Costa）负责总体规划，建筑师奥斯卡·尼迈耶（Oscar Niemeyer）设计所有公共建筑，景观设计师罗伯托·布雷尔·马克斯负责绿化设计。这座新首都的建设创造了建筑史上的奇迹：

**建设数据**：
- **建设周期**：41个月（1957年2月开工，1960年4月21日落成）
- **人力动员**：来自巴西各地约30,000名工人，多数来自东北部
- **机械投入**：200多台机器24小时作业
- **地理位置**：选在巴西地理中心附近，从无到有建在热带稀树草原上

库比契克的建都不仅是一个建筑工程项目，更是国家重建的象征。新首都很快发挥了重要作用：
- 连接巴西广袤领土的交通网络得到发展

- **国家整合**：通过首都建设促进领土统一和地区平衡
- **文化自信**：用现代建筑语言表达拉丁美洲的独立精神

### **第三代（20世纪后期）：国家整合的追求者（阿布贾，1976年至今）**

尼日利亚的迁都进程始于1976年，当时该国刚刚经历内战结束7年。军事政府的穆尔塔拉·穆罕默德将军决定将首都从沿海的大城市拉各斯迁往内陆中心地带的阿布贾。这一决定背后的逻辑是：

- **主要设计师：** 卢西奥·科斯塔（城市规划）和奥斯卡·尼迈耶（建筑）

**迁都原因：**
- 开发巴西内陆地区，发展国家地理中心
- 减轻沿海城市的人口压力
- 体现国家现代化雄心
- 促进内陆经济发展

**特色成果：**
- 城市布局呈飞机形状，极具现代主义特色
- 建筑被联合国教科文组织列为世界文化遗产
- 建筑作品如巴西利亚大教堂、巴西国会大厦成为标志性建筑

### 2. **阿布贾 - 非洲的迁都范例**

**时间与过程：**
- **1976年：** 成立联邦首都特区
- **1991年12月12日：** 正式成为尼日利亚首都
- **从以下城市迁出：** 拉各斯

**迁都原因：**
- **民族平衡：** 拉各斯位于南方基督教区，为平衡北方穆斯林地区而选择地理中心
- **国家统一：** 内战后需要通过地理中心的首都强化国家认同
- **战略安全：** 沿海城市存在安全风险
- **分散发展：** 避免过度集中在沿海地区

### 3. **华盛顿特区 - 现代首都规划样板**

**时间与设计师：**
- **1790年：** 通过《居住法案》决定建立新首都
- **设计师：** 皮埃尔·查尔斯·朗方（法裔美国建筑师）
- **从以下城市临时迁出：** 费城）

**设立原因：**
- **政治中立：** 建立独立于任何州的联邦特区
- **南北平衡：** 在南北之间的妥协选择
- **国家象征：** 体现新生美国的民主理念

### **政治因素**
- 民族平衡和地区团结
- 政治中立性
- 国家统一的需要

### **经济因素** 
- 开发落后地区
- 促进区域平衡发展
- 缓解大城市压力

### **战略因素**
- 国防安全考虑
- 地理中心位置的优势
- 避免沿海城市的脆弱性

### **象征因素**
- 现代化国家形象的塑造
- 新的历史开始的标志
- 国家愿景的物化表达

这些迁都案例表明，城市迁址和新区规划往往与重大的国家发展战略密切相关，体现了不同时期的历史使命和发展理念。每个案例都是国家治理智慧的体现，通过空间重新布局来解决复杂的社会政治问题。

* Al-Karamah was intended to be the permanent capital of the United Arab Emirates located between Abu Dhabi and Dubai, but it was never built.[14]
* Viedma, the capital of the Río Negro Province, was proposed by President Raúl Alfonsín as a new capital for Argentina in 1986, replacing Buenos Aires. <document>
<title>Edwin Lutyens</title>
<fragment>
Largely designed by Lutyens over 20 or so years (1912 to 1930), New Delhi, situated within the metropolis of Delhi, popularly known as 'Lutyens' Delhi', was chosen to replace Calcutta as the seat of the British Indian government in 1912;[28] the project was completed in 1929 and officially inaugurated in 1931. In undertaking this project, Lutyens invented his own new order of classical architecture, which has become known as the Delhi Order and was used by him for several designs in England, such as Campion Hall, Oxford. Unlike the more traditional British architects who came before him, he was both inspired by and incorporated various features from the local and traditional Indian architecture—something most clearly seen in the great drum-mounted Buddhist dome of Viceroy's House, now Rashtrapati Bhavan. This palatial building, containing 340 rooms, is built on an area of some 330 acres (130 ha) and incorporates a private garden also designed by Lutyens. 
</fragment>

<document>
<title>Lúcio Costa</title>
<fragment>

The idea to establish a new Brazilian capital was adopted, and the location for Brasília would be within the Brazilian State of Goiás. The search for the site had been calculated, based on factors such as the favorability of the climate, water supply, land quality for agriculture, a suitable power source within 100 kilometers, and access to ground and air transportation.



### Costa's Design

[edit]

Once it had been determined that there would be a new capital and the location had been established, the project entered into the design process. The plan was to be selected among competing plans from various Brazilian architects and city planners by an international jury. The participating designers were given the necessary information to make suitable plans for the space. Each participant was to submit two pieces in their proposal, a basic layout of the city and a supporting report that exhibited logistical details.


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Murtala Muhammed</title>
<fragment>
Muhammed took federal control of the country's two largest newspapers – Daily Times and New Nigerian; all media in Nigeria was now under federal control. He also took federal control of the remaining state-run universities.[29] On February 3, 1976, the Military Government of Murtala Muhammed created new states and renamed others, the states he created include: Bauchi, Benue, Borno, Imo, Niger, Ogun, and Ondo.[30] This brought the total number of states in Nigeria to nineteen in 1976.


As head of state, Muhammed put in place plans to build a new Federal Capital Territory due to Lagos being overcrowded. He set up a panel headed by Justice Akinola Aguda, which chose the Abuja area as the new capital ahead of other proposed locations. On 3 February 1976, Muhammed announced that the Federal Capital would in the future move to a federal territory location of about 8,000 square kilometres in the central part of the country.[29]


</fragment>
<fragment>

However his highly popular, often televised "with immediate effect" style of governing, also gained some criticism amongst the countries top civil servants - some of which were Nigeria’s top intellectuals.[27] His ad-hoc Presidential proclamations left his civil service often unprepared, lacking details or even funding to implement his ideas, and his administration led to the dismissal of thousands of civil servants.[27] Over 10,000 civil servants, government employees were dismissed without benefits; reasons stated were age, health, incompetence, or malpractice. The removal of such a large amount of public officials affected the public service, the judiciary, the police and armed forces, the diplomatic service, public corporations, and university officials. Quite a few officials were tried on corruption charges, and an ex-military state governor was executed for gross office misconduct.[28]

Based on my research using Wikipedia sources, I can provide you with a comprehensive analysis of capital city transfers and their economic development rationales, with specific examples from the countries you mentioned.

## Strategic Rationale for Capital City Transfers

The decisions to establish new capital cities have been driven by several key economic development objectives:

### 1. **Regional Economic Rebalancing**
- **Decentralization of economic activity**: New capitals are strategically positioned to redistribute economic activity away from dominant coastal economic centers
- **Interior development goals**: Moving capitals inland stimulates development in previously neglected regions

### 2. **Long-term Economic Planning**
- **Population management**: Relocating capitals addresses overcrowding and infrastructure constraints in existing economic centers
- **Infrastructure modernization**: New capitals allow for implementation of modern urban planning and technological infrastructure

### 3. **Economic Efficiency and Governance**
- **Reduced congestion**: Alleviating pressure on infrastructure and services in existing economic hubs
- **Improved administrative efficiency**: Purpose-built capitals can optimize government operations and economic regulation

## Case Studies from Your Examples

### **Brasília, Brazil (1956-1960)**
- **Economic driver**: President Juscelino Kubitschek's vision to open Brazil's interior to development
- **Planning rationale**: Selection based on climate, water supply, agricultural land quality, and transportation access
- **Economic impact**: Successfully created a new economic hub in central Brazil, reducing Rio de Janeiro's dominance 
- **Design approach**: Lúcio Costa's modernist plan for a planned city, with Oscar Niemeyer's architectural vision

### **Abuja, Nigeria (1976-present)**
- **Economic motivation**: Murtala Muhammed's government sought to address Lagos's overcrowding and establish a centrally located capital
- **Selection process**: Justice Akinola Aguda panel chose Abuja to create a federal capital territory in Nigeria's central region
- **Economic goal**: Create a more balanced national economy by developing Nigeria's interior regions
- **Implementation**: Gradual transfer of government functions to stimulate new economic center

### **New Delhi, India (1912-1931)**
- **Economic context**: British decision to move capital from Calcutta to address growing economic and political aspirations in northern India
- **Economic planning**: Edwin Lutyens designed a new administrative center over 20 years, completed in 1929
- **Economic integration**: Incorporated traditional Indian architectural elements while creating modern administrative infrastructure
- **Economic outcome**: Created a new economic and administrative hub in North India

### **Dodoma, Tanzania (1973-present)**
- **Economic philosophy**: Julius Nyerere's move from Dar es Salaam aligned with Ujamaa socialism and rural development goals
- **Economic rationale**: Promote development away from the coastal economic center toward Tanzania's interior
- **Planning approach**: International competition for master plan, with Canadian firm Project Planning Associates selected
- **Economic timeline**: Planned for 400,000 residents by 2000 and 1.3 million by 2020

## Economic Development Outcomes

### **Successes:**
- **Regional development**: New capitals have successfully stimulated investment and population growth in previously undeveloped regions
- **Infrastructure modernization**: Purpose-built capitals incorporate modern economic infrastructure and urban planning
- **Economic diversification**: Reduced economic concentration in traditional coastal commercial centers

### **Challenges:**
- **High implementation costs**: New capital construction requires massive public investment
- **Economic transition periods**: Gradual economic shifts rather than immediate relocations
- **Infrastructure development timelines**: Long periods required to build full economic ecosystems

## Contemporary Economic Relevance

The rationale for capital transfers continues to be relevant for:
- **Developing economies** seeking regional balance
- **Countries facing coastal overcrowding** and congestion
- **Nations pursuing long-term economic restructuring** through strategic infrastructure investment

These examples demonstrate that capital city transfers are fundamentally economic development strategies aimed at creating more balanced, efficient, and sustainable national economies through strategic spatial planning and investment redistribution.

Based on my research, here are the major planned capital cities that were deliberately chosen and constructed, along with their planning rationale:

## **Brasília, Brazil (1956-1960)**

**Rio de Janeiro's Limitations:**
- Coastal location concentrated economic activity
- Geographic constraints on expansion
- Desire to integrate Brazil's vast interior into national development

**Planning Process:**
- President Juscelino Kubitschek's ambitious five-year development plan ("50 anos de progresso em 5")
- Location chosen for central location, temperate climate, water availability, and agricultural potential
- Lúcio Costa won the master plan competition with his "Plano Piloto" - a modernist plan of two intersecting axes forming an airplane shape
- Oscar Niemeyer designed the iconic modernist architecture

**Design Philosophy:**
- Modernist efficiency with zoning for government, residential, commercial, and cultural areas
- Monumental scale to project Brazil's emergence as a modern power
- Integration with natural landscape

## **Abuja, Nigeria (1976-present)**

**Lagos's Limitations:**
- Extreme overcrowding and congestion on small island geography
- Severe infrastructure strain
- Ethnic and political tensions in economically dominant coastal region

**Planning Process:**
- Military government under Murtala Muhammed appointed Justice Akinola Aguda panel
- Nine potential sites evaluated on geographic centrality, availability of land, ethnic neutrality, climate, and proximity to transport
- Location chosen for central position, ethnic neutrality, and development potential
- International Design Associates (Japanese-American consortium) won planning competition

**Design Philosophy:**
- Federal district model with separation of government functions
- Infrastructure built to accommodate rapid population growth
- Modern facilities integrated with Nigerian cultural elements

## **New Delhi, India (1912-1931)**

**Calcutta's Limitations:**
- Distance from major Indian population centers
- Rising political and nationalist sentiment in Calcutta
- Strategic positioning after British capital moved from Delhi to Calcutta in 1911

**Planning Process:**
- Edwin Lutyens led the architectural design team
- Herbert Baker designed key government buildings
- Planned as a "garden city" with wide boulevards, monuments, and modern infrastructure

**Design Philosophy:**
- Imperial grandeur with Indian architectural elements
- Green belt integration and monumentality
- Separation of native and European areas (later dismantled)

## **Dodoma, Tanzania (1973-present)**

**Dar es Salaam's Limitations:**
- Coastal colonial history
- Population overwhelm of basic services
- Desire to promote Ujamaa socialism and rural development

**Planning Process:**
- Julius Nyerere's socialist development vision emphasized interior development
- International competition for master plan - won by Canadian firm Project Planning Associates
- Gradual transfer of government functions至今 continues

**Design Philosophy:**
- Socialist planning principles
- Agricultural integration
- Community-focused neighborhoods

## **Additional Major Examples:**

**Canberra, Australia (1913-present)**
- Compromise between Sydney and Melbourne
- Walter Burley Griffin's garden city design integrated with natural topography

**Islamabad, Pakistan (1960-present)**
- Karachi's congestion and coastal vulnerability
- Greek firm Doxiadis Associates' hierarchical planning system
- Terraced design with green space integration

**Putrajaya, Malaysia (1995-present)**
- Kuala Lumpur's congestion
- Islamic architectural elements integrated with modern infrastructure
- Garden city concept with extensive waterfront development

## **Common Planning Elements:**

1. **Strategic Location Choice** - Geographic centrality, development potential, ethnic neutrality
2. **Modern Infrastructure** - State-of-the-art facilities for the planning era
3. **Cultural Integration** - Fusing global planning principles with national architectural identity
4. **Economic Development Focus** - Creating new regional growth poles
5. **Long Implementation Timelines** - Decades required for full development and government transfer

These planned capitals represent ambitious national projects aimed at transforming geographic and economic landscapes, though many faced challenges including cost overruns, gradual rather than immediate implementation, and the struggle to build complete urban ecosystems from scratch.

Based on a comprehensive comparison of global megacities, here are the key similarities and differences among cities like Moscow, London, Tokyo, Bangkok, and Kinshasa:

## **Key Similarities**

**Geographic & Economic Status:**
- All are major national capitals or dominant urban centers in their respective countries
- Each is classified as a "megacity" (urban area with populations typically exceeding 10 million)
- All serve as primary economic, political, and cultural hubs for their regions

**Urban Challenges:**
- Face similar infrastructure pressures from massive populations
- Deal with transportation, housing, and service delivery challenges
- Experience rapid urbanization and metropolitan area expansion

## **Key Differences**

**Geographic Distribution & Regional Context:**
- **Northern Hemisphere**: Moscow (Russia), London (UK), Tokyo (Japan)
- **Tropical/Subtropical**: Bangkok (Thailand), Kinshasa (DRC)
- **Cultural Realms**: European (Moscow, London), East Asian (Tokyo), Southeast Asian (Bangkok), Central African (Kinshasa)

**Historical Development:**
- **Ancient foundations**: Moscow, London, Tokyo have long urban histories
- **Colonial legacy**: London as imperial center, Bangkok as never-colonized Asian monarchy, Kinshasa as colonial creation (formerly Leopoldville)
- **Modern emergence**: Bangkok and Kinshasa experienced explosive growth in recent decades

**Global Rankings & Stature:**
From the World's 50 most-populous urban areas:
1. **Tokyo** - Ranked #1 globally
2. **Bangkok** - Ranked #16 globally 
3. **Moscow** - Ranked #18 globally
4. **London** - Ranked #39 globally
5. **Kinshasa** - Ranked #30 globally (combined Kinshasa-Brazzaville area)

**Economic Structure:**
- **Tokyo/London**: Global financial centers with advanced service economies
- **Moscow**: Resource-based economy transitioning to services
- **Bangkok**: Manufacturing hub with growing service sector
- **Kinshasa**: Developing economy with informal sector dominance

**Infrastructure Quality:**
- **Tokyo/London**: World-class public transportation and infrastructure
- **Moscow**: Comprehensive but aging Soviet-era infrastructure
- **Bangkok**: Rapidly modernizing but strained infrastructure
- **Kinshasa**: Severe infrastructure challenges and limited service coverage

## **Distinctive Characteristics**

- **Tokyo**: World's largest urban area, technological innovation leader
- **London**: Global financial center, historic metropolitan area
- **Moscow**: Largest European city by population, former Soviet capital
- **Bangkok**: Southeast Asian gateway, tropical climate challenges
- **Kinshasa**: One of Africa's largest cities, faces significant development challenges

While these cities share the designation of being megacities, they differ dramatically in terms of development level, global influence, infrastructure quality, and the specific challenges they face as urban centers in the 21st century.

Based on my research of world capitals, here are some prominent examples of **planned capital cities that were purpose-built as administrative/political centers**:

## Major Planned Capital Cities:

### **Asia**
- **Islamabad, Pakistan** - Built in the 1960s as a planned city to replace Karachi as Pakistan's capital. Notable for its high standards of living, safety, cleanliness, abundant greenery and organized architecture.

- **Putrajaya, Malaysia** - Built in the 1990s as the new federal administrative center, complementing Kuala Lumpur as the co-capital.

### **Africa**
- **Abuja, Nigeria** - Constructed mainly in the 1980s based on a master plan by International Planning Associates. It replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital on December 12, 1991.

- **Pretoria, South Africa** - One of South Africa's three capital cities, established as the administrative capital.

### **South America**
- **Brasília, Brazil** - Built in the late 1950s and inaugurated as the capital in 1960. Famous for its modernist architecture designed by Oscar Niemeyer.

### **Oceania**
- **Canberra, Australia** - Founded following the federation of Australia as the national seat of government. It's Australia's largest inland city and was specifically planned for this purpose.

### **Other Examples**:
- **Washington, D.C., USA** - Established as the federal capital in the late 18th century
- **New Delhi, India** - Built in the early 20th century by the British as the new imperial capital
- **Astana/Nur-Sultan, Kazakhstan** - Became the capital in 1997 after being significantly developed

These planned capitals share common characteristics: organized urban layouts, government-centric architecture, and development focused on administrative efficiency rather than organic growth. Many were created to replace overcrowded existing capitals or to symbolically represent new national identities.

<title>Federal District (Brazil)</title>
<fragment>

The capital of Brazil was transferred from Rio de Janeiro to Brasília on 21 April 1960 and its new territory, split off from Goiás state on the border with the Minas Gerais state, became the current Federal District. After the transfer the old Federal District, containing the city of Rio de Janeiro, became the state of Guanabara. This state existed from 1960 until 1975, when it merged with the state of Rio de Janeiro. With the merger the capital of Rio de Janeiro state was transferred back from Niterói to Rio de Janeiro itself (as it had been until 1834 when the empire created the Neutral Municipality).

The Federal Capital Territory was created upon the promulgation of decree number 6 of 1976. It came into existence due to a need to find a replacement for the capital city of Lagos, which had become congested and had little space for expansion. The area chosen as the new capital was principally Gwari Land (the home of the tribes referred to as the Gbagyis, their language is referred to as Gwari) with high concentrations of Muslims and Christians and high degree of neutrality from the dominant ethnic groups.[6]


Decree 6 of 1976, gave the federal government rights over land within the territory. The population density prior to the takeover by the government was sparse with a population of 120,000 residents living in 840 villages and mostly of Gwari heritage.[6] Inhabitants were relocated to nearby towns like Suleja in Niger state, and New Karshi in Nasarawa State on the outskirts of the territory.

Historical aspects of the capital cities of Japan

The **capital of Japan** is Tokyo.[1][2][3] Throughout history, the national capital has been in locations other than Tokyo.




## History

[edit]

Traditionally, the home of the Emperor is considered the capital. From 794 through 1868, the Emperor lived in Heian-kyō, modern-day Kyoto.[4][5] After 1868, the seat of the Government of Japan and the location of the Emperor's home was moved to Edo, which it renamed Tokyo.[6]


In 1941, the Ministry of Education published the "designation of Tokyo as capital" (東京奠都, *Tōkyō-tento*).[7]

<document>
<title>Geography of Beijing</title>
<fragment>
Downtown Beijing has several lakes called *hai* or sea. During the Yuan dynasty, the Mongol rulers expanded them and built imperial palace of Dadu around them. Subsequent emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties used the lakes as imperial gardens. Today, the three northernmost lakes, *Xihai* (West Sea), *Houhai* (Rear Sea) and *Qianhai* (Front Sea), collectively known as *Shichahai*, are lined with bars and cafés and known for nightlife. To their south, *Beihai* (North Sea) is a city park, and *Zhonghai* (Central Sea) and *Nanhai* (South Sea) are part of the Zhongnanhai Compound, residence to China's leaders. This string of lakes used to form the main riverbed of the Yongding River, which now flows 50–60 km (31–37 mi) to the west. But 1,800 years ago, the Yongding flowed through Jishuitan and downtown Beijing and then into Longtan Lake and on to Tongzhou.[6] A major flood in 295 A.D. devastated part of Beijing, then known as Ji.

<title>Soan River</title>
<fragment>

The Soan river is more than 250 kilometres (160 mi) long. The Islamabad Highway crosses this stream near Sihala at the Kak Pul bridge. The Ling Stream joins the Soan river just before the Kak Pul. Two other streams, the Korang River and the Lai stream, join the Soan just before and after the Soan Bridge, respectively. After following a path along a big curve, the stream reaches the Kalabagh proposed Dam Site close to Pir Piai where it falls into the Indus river.[1]


The marine life of the river are currently endangered due to the discharge of chemicals of the Sihala Industrial State and effluent water of Rawalpindi city into it.[3][*better source needed*]

<document>
<title>Yongding River</title>
<fragment>
The **Yongding River** (Chinese: 永定河; pinyin: *Yǒngdìng Hé*; Wade–Giles: *Yungting He*) is a river in northern China. It is one of the main tributaries in the Hai River system and is best known as the largest river to flow through Beijing. In recent years, the Beijing segment of the river has dried up due to environmental issues.[1] The Beijing municipal government has invested 16 billion yuan in an effort to replace the riverbed with parkland or smaller bodies of water.[2]




## Etymology

[edit]

The river was originally called **Wuding River** (Chinese: 無定河; pinyin: *Wúdìng Hé*), literally "unfixed river", because its flow was irregular. When the Kangxi Emperor reigned, he enacted various hydraulic engineering projects in the region to rein in the seasonal flooding. After those projects, the river was renamed to its modern name, which means "ever-fixed river".[3]



## Geography

[edit]

**Hindon River** is an Indian river in that originates from the Shakumbhari devi range (Upper Sivaliks) in Saharanpur district of Uttar Pradesh and falls into Yamuna river in Noida. Hindon is a tributary of Yamuna and is entirely rainfed, having an approximate catchment area of 7,083 square kilometres (2,735 sq mi).

## **Five Most Populous Countries & Their Capitals (2023)**

**1st: India** - **New Delhi**
- Population: ~1.42 billion
- **Major Rivers:** 
  - Yamuna River (primary major river flowing through Delhi)
  - Hindon River (400km tributary of the Yamuna)

**2nd: China** - **Beijing**
- Population: ~1.41 billion  
- **Major Rivers:**
  - Yongding River (largest river flowing through Beijing, though largely dried up in recent years)
  - Historical riverbed lakes (Xihai, Houhai, Qianhai, Beihai, Zhonghai, Nanhai)

**3rd: United States** - **Washington, D.C.**
- Population: ~334 million
- **Major Rivers:**
  - Potomac River (forms Washington's southwestern border)
  - Anacostia River (8.4-mile tributary flowing into the Potomac)

**4th: Indonesia** - **Jakarta**
- Population: ~279 million
- **Major Rivers:**
  - Ciliwung River (119km river flowing through Jakarta from Mount Pangrango to North Jakarta)

**5th: Pakistan** - **Islamabad**
- Population: ~241 million
- **Major Rivers:**
  - Soan River (250km+ long, flows through Islamabad area, joins the Indus River)
  - Korang River (tributary joining the Soan River)
  - Lai stream (another tributary joining the Soan)

## **Key Notes:**
- India became the world's most populous country in April 2023, surpassing China for the first time
- Beijing's Yongding River has been severely affected by drought and water management issues
- Islamabad's river system predominantly feeds into the larger Soan River watershed
- Jakarta's Ciliwung River historically played a crucial role in the city's settlement and development
